verses.translation_literal: A song of the ascents. Those who trust in YHWH are like Mount Zion: it will not be shaken; for ever it sits.
verses.translation_dramatic: A song for the climbing. Those who lean their whole weight on the LORD are like Mount Zion itself: it does not shake, it does not stagger. Age after age, it simply sits there.
verses.directors_commentary:
The opening words give the heading, "song of the ascents": a title shared by fifteen psalms, most likely sung by pilgrims climbing up to Jerusalem for the feasts, though the exact sense of ma'alot, "steps" or "goings-up", is not certain. The KJV's "degrees" is an old word for steps, which now sounds like an academic honour, and hides the picture of people walking uphill singing.

The point of the verse is a comparison between a person and a mountain. The verb bataḥ means to rest your weight on something, to be at ease because you are held up. The mountain "will not be shaken" (lo yimmot), and the same verb is used in other psalms for a foot that slips. A people who sit in a high place, with a hill beneath them and a god above them, can say the ground will not move. The last word is yeshev, "sits", the plain Hebrew verb for sitting or living in a house. The KJV makes the verse a promise ("shall be as") and puts "cannot be removed" for a verb that only says "will not be shaken"; the Hebrew has no "shall" and no "cannot". Play it as a statement of fact, said by people who are physically standing on the thing they are describing. Rashi and Metzudat David read it as a comparison between trusting people and the mountain; Ibn Ezra reads it as looking to the future.

philological_notes.note: From the root 'to go up'. The title of fifteen psalms, probably for pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem, though the origin of the phrase is not settled. The Targum on this verse reads it as 'ascents of the deep' and attaches a different tradition to it.
Participle: 'those who are trusting'. The root describes being at rest because something holds you up, not a one-time act of belief. It sets up the picture of the unmoving mountain.
'To totter, be shaken'. It is used for feet that slip and for earth that gives way, so the sense is wobbling and not only being 'removed' as in the KJV.

verses.translation_literal: Jerusalem: mountains [are] round about her, and YHWH [is] round about his people, from now and until for ever.
verses.translation_dramatic: Jerusalem. Look at her: the mountains stand round about her, ridge behind ridge, closing her in. And the LORD stands round about his people, just so, from this moment and on and on, until there is no more time to count.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse is the picture the first verse promised. Jerusalem sits on a ridge, with the Mount of Olives to the east, the hills of the Hinnom valley to the south and west, and higher ground beyond. A traveller coming up for a feast would see the ring of hills close in on the city. The psalmist says that God stands in the same relation to his people as those hills do to the city, a wall that is also a gaze looking inward.

The KJV adds "As ... so", which makes a tidy comparison. The Hebrew has only two clauses side by side, with the word "round about" (saviv) used twice, once for the hills and once for YHWH, so the repetition is the whole argument. Say the word both times with the same weight. The final phrase "from now and until for ever" (me'attah ve'ad olam) has a deliberate edge: it begins in the present, with the pilgrims standing there, and has no end. Radak points out that mountains alone never protected Jerusalem, because enemies took the city even with them there, so the safety comes from God and not from the geography. Malbim makes the same argument in the other direction: the city's natural defence is only the hills, so the people who trust in God have more than that.

philological_notes.note: 'Round about, all around', used twice, so that the hills and YHWH are matched. The word describes a ring, not a single side.
A fixed phrase: 'from now and until for ever'. Meiri reads 'from then', as if the promise started at a later time; the plain sense is that it begins at the time of speaking.

verses.translation_literal: For the sceptre of wickedness will not rest upon the lot of the righteous, so that the righteous may not send out their hands in injustice.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the rod of the wicked will not settle and stay upon the land that the righteous were given by lot. The LORD will not let it lie there, so that the righteous never reach out their own hands to do wrong.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse moves from the hills to politics. A shevet is a staff, and it is also the sign of a ruler: the same word is used for a shepherd's rod, a king's sceptre, and the rod of discipline. The "sceptre of wickedness" is a wicked government, the rule of foreign powers, or a wicked ruler. The KJV's "rod" keeps the staff but loses the political sense; the ASV's "sceptre" is closer. Metzudat Zion notes that shevet means rule, because the ruler holds the staff, and cites Genesis 49:10.

The "lot" (goral) is the land that each family received by casting lots when Israel settled, so it means the inheritance, the family's piece of ground, and more than "fate". An audience in a country where land was identity would hear this as a promise that foreign rulers will not stay on their fields.

The second half gives the reason, and it is the surprising part. The KJV's "lest the righteous put forth their hands unto iniquity" is correct in sense, but the Hebrew picture is of hands stretched out: if the wicked stay in power too long, even honest people will reach out to do wrong, since they will think crime is how the world works. The Hebrew uses lema'an, "in order that", which is purposeful, so God removes the scepter with this aim. Metzudat David says the same: the righteous would otherwise follow the wicked, seeing them prosper for a long time. Play it as a worry, with the stakes on the hearers' own hands.

philological_notes.note: A staff, a rod, a sceptre; also a tribe. Here it is the sign of rule, not simply a stick, so 'sceptre' fits the political sense.
The 'lot', literally the pebble or token cast to divide land among families. It stands for the inheritance itself, which is why the verse is about territory.
'Send out their hands': an idiom for reaching out to act, usually to take or to strike. English 'put forth' is flatter than the picture of hands sent out.
'Injustice, wrong'. The ending -ah is an archaic form of the noun, not a pronoun; the KJV's 'iniquity' is a fair, though churchy, rendering.

verses.translation_literal: Do good, O YHWH, to the good, and to the upright in their hearts.
verses.translation_dramatic: Do good, O LORD, to the ones who are good, to the ones whose hearts run straight.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from description to prayer. After three verses of statement the speaker now speaks directly to God, in the imperative. The verb heitivah (from yatav) and the word for "good" in the next word (tov) are related roots and sound alike, so the Hebrew plays on them: "do-good to the good". The KJV keeps this in "Do good ... unto those that be good", and gets it right, though the words "that be" are old-fashioned.

The second half is where the weight falls. "Upright" (yesharim) means straight, level, the opposite of the "twisting" ways in the next verse, and "in their hearts" says where the straightness is found. The Hebrew has no verb or "that are", and the KJV's "that are upright in their hearts" is a smooth addition. Ibn Ezra notes that uprightness is in the heart and is the root from which words and deeds are built, and Radak splits the two halves, with the good in their deeds and the upright in their hearts. Play the line quietly, as the shortest verse of the psalm and a turn in tone.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of 'to be good', with the added ending -ah that gives a pleading tone. From yatav, a related root to tov 'good' in the next word: a sound-play on the word for good.
'Straight' and 'in their hearts': the straightness is inward. Radak reads the good as good in deeds and the upright as upright in their hearts; Ibn Ezra stresses that uprightness starts in the heart.

verses.translation_literal: And those who turn aside their twisting ways, YHWH will lead them away with the doers of iniquity. Peace upon Israel!
verses.translation_dramatic: But those who bend aside onto their own crooked paths, the LORD will march them away with the workers of wrong. And over Israel, peace.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm closes with a sharp contrast. The word "crooked" is aqalqal, a rare and rough-sounding word that is itself crooked: four syllables that wind back on themselves. It occurs in Judges 5:6 for the winding paths that travellers took when roads were unsafe, which Metzudat Zion cites in this verse. The KJV's "crooked ways" is accurate. The verb "turn aside" (hammatim) is a participle and means those who bend their own road away from the straight one, so the choice is theirs.

The verb yolikhem, "he will lead them", is the verb for leading a captive procession. The KJV's "lead them forth" is mild; the sense is a march into exile or punishment, and the Targum explicitly makes it Gehenna. The KJV, like this translation, reads 'et as "with" and not as the object marker, so that the wicked are taken off to share the end of the workers of iniquity. Radak thinks this means the wicked in Israel will be removed, and then Israel will have peace; Ibn Ezra reads it as a prayer. The last two words, shalom al Yisrael, have no verb. They can be a blessing or a statement, and the dramatic reading picks a calm, certain close. The same phrase ends Psalm 128. A wish at the end of a psalm sung by walking pilgrims would be heard as a benediction.

philological_notes.note: A rare reduplicated form meaning 'twisting, winding'. It occurs in Judges 5:6 for winding paths. The sound of the word imitates its meaning.
Hiphil of 'to walk': 'he will make them go', the verb for leading away a body of people. The Targum reads this as Gehenna.
'Doers of iniquity': a fixed expression for evildoers in the psalms. 'Aven' covers trouble, wickedness and idols, and is wider than the KJV's 'iniquity'.
